newsitem.title: UK: Major discourages British election fever.
newsitem.headline: Major discourages British election fever.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major discouraged the notion that he was about to call a snap election, saying people should stay cool amid feverish speculation about a polling date.

"There is a general election in the near future, of course there is. But I think people should just sit back and relax and not get overexcited about it for the moment," Major told Sky television in an interview on Thursday.
His move appeared designed to dispel the idea that he was travelling to Wales on Friday to tell members of his Conservative Party that they faced a general election on March 20.
Major will make a keynote speech to the annual Welsh conference of his Conservative Party at about 1300 GMT in the border village of Holywell near Chester.

The event was moved forward from June to enable him to use it to announce a March poll if he should choose to do so. The election must be held by May 20 and the hot favourite -- reported for several weeks to be Major's preferred date -- is May 1.

The opposition Labour Party, leading in national opinion polls by about 20 percentage points, is planning a parliamentary ambush on Major next Monday when it will move a vote of censure in Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg.
The vote is effectively a demand for the resignation of the man who has piloted Britain's attempts to have a European Union ban on beef exports lifted following the "mad cow" disease crisis.

A successful vote is seen as a remote possibility. Although Major lacks an overall parliamentary majority, for Labour to win Monday's vote it would need strong backing from minority parties in the House of Commons.
But should it happen, there could be a confidence vote the following day and defeat for Major would force an election.
The parliamentary arithmetic is further complicated by a by-election in the constituency of Wirral South, a few miles (km) across the River Dee from Holywell.
It has been called for February 27 following the death of legislator Barry Porter. Polls indicate Labour is poised to grab the seat which Porter won by over 8,000 votes at the 1992 general election.
This would not merely give Labour leader Tony Blair a massive fillip ahead of the general election, but also plunge Major into a minority in the House of Commons.
If Major's speech on Friday proves an anti-climax as far as an election date is concerned, the prime minister is expected to use it to slam Labour's plans for mini-parliaments for Scotland and Wales.
Conservatives claim that the idea could presage a break-up of the United Kingdom and plan to stress constitutional issues during the election campaign.
Major has decided to take the unusual step of personally opening a debate in parliament on constitutional issues next Thursday.
